intro: Augustine examines why knowing what we ought to do can leave us unable to do it, and why our own minds remain difficult to understand. This profile moves from his importance to desire, memory, will and time, then tests the theological interpretation and offers a route into his texts.
description: Explore Augustine on divided will, memory, time, and grace, with a critical reading of how inward experience supports—or fails to support—theology.

sections.heading: Why knowing the good does not settle how to live
paragraphs: Augustine gives sustained philosophical attention to a familiar failure: being convinced that a change is right while continuing to resist it. In Confessions VIII, his difficulty is no longer simply uncertainty about what to believe. He describes established attachments competing with a commitment he endorses. The account challenges an explanation of wrongdoing that rests only on ignorance: better information may leave a divided person divided.

The religious setting matters. Augustine writes as a Christian reflecting on his earlier life, drawing on and disputing inherited philosophical traditions. His descriptions of memory, desire and choice are embedded in prayer, not presented as a neutral psychological experiment. Their philosophical value need not depend on accepting every conclusion he draws from them, but separating the observations from the interpretation requires attention to both.

This distinction explains a continuing philosophical use of his work. In a dispute about responsibility, it matters whether someone lacks knowledge, acts under external compulsion, or acts from habits they also want to overcome. Augustine makes the third possibility difficult to ignore. His account also raises a further question: if moral renewal requires divine assistance, what responsibility remains with the person? That question leads from the inward narrative to the disputed relation between grace and freedom.
listItems: Historical setting: Late antique Christianity and the philosophical traditions Augustine encounters shape his questions about truth, evil and the good life. His inward inquiry remains a conversation with these traditions.
Signature contribution: Memory, will, love, sin and grace become subjects of connected argument. Augustine asks how a person can know, remember and choose while remaining partly opaque to themselves.

Influence trail: His writings supply arguments and vocabulary for later Christian disputes over freedom and grace. Their continued use should be assessed through those specific problems rather than a claim that he invented introspection.

Historical setting in the text: The converted narrator of Confessions interprets his earlier conflicts retrospectively. A convincing account of what a conflict felt like does not by itself establish the narrator’s explanation of its cause.

Influence as a question: Distinguishing voluntary action from an undivided will helps explain why choice, habit and responsibility remain separate issues. Whether grace resolves their tension is a further debate.

sections.heading: Desire, memory, will and the experience of time
paragraphs: These concepts describe different kinds of dependence. Desire concerns what we seek; memory concerns how what is absent remains available to thought; will concerns commitments and action; time concerns how a changing life can be experienced as connected. Augustine relates these questions to God, but the connections need arguments. Dissatisfaction with one achievement, for example, does not by itself demonstrate that an infinite object of desire exists.

The discussion of memory in Confessions X resists the idea that inward access makes us fully transparent to ourselves. Augustine describes bringing images and knowledge to mind, struggling to retrieve what is hidden, and wondering at a capacity he cannot fully grasp. This is an inquiry into remembering and self-understanding, not a claim to have discovered a modern theory of unconscious mental processing.

In Confessions XI, reciting a familiar song illustrates how temporal experience holds together. Before singing, we anticipate it; while singing, attention moves through it; afterward, what was anticipated is remembered. The example distinguishes the event from our present awareness of its absent parts. It helps explain how we experience a duration without having every moment before us at once; it is not, by itself, a demonstration that the external world or physical time is unreal.
listItems: Restless desire: Augustine interprets the search for lasting fulfillment as directed toward God. Distinguish his theological account of its proper end from the experience of dissatisfaction that a reader may recognize without sharing that account.

Memory: The self is layered, strange, and not fully transparent to itself. A remembered sorrow can be contemplated without feeling that sorrow in the same way; remembering a state and presently undergoing it differ.
Will: Moral failure is not just ignorance; it involves divided love. Rival inclinations can belong to one person: Augustine rejects treating every conflict as evidence for two separate souls.
Time: Memory, attention and expectation make past, present and future available in different ways. Calling a memory present does not make the remembered event present again.

Historical pressure: Grace is God’s assistance in willing and doing good. Augustine’s account of that assistance makes the relation between dependence and responsibility especially difficult; it cannot be reduced to ordinary advice to try harder.

sections.heading: Does inward conflict warrant the theological answer?
paragraphs: The strongest objection concerns a transition in the argument: an illuminating description of human conflict does not establish a uniquely Christian explanation of it. Recognizing divided desire may support an account in terms of habits, competing commitments or social formation. Further reasons are needed to show that inherited sin and divine grace best explain the condition. Otherwise the interpretation risks supplying the answer before alternatives receive a fair hearing.

Augustine’s reply is stronger than “my life felt this way.” His account belongs to a larger case involving scripture, arguments about God and the good, and a religious community’s practices. In On Grace and Free Will, he maintains both the need for grace and the reality of human willing. Assistance, on this account, makes good willing possible rather than making willing irrelevant. Yet a critic can still ask why people are blameworthy for failures they cannot remedy without assistance they cannot secure by themselves.

A contemporary test can preserve the original objection without pretending to reproduce a conversion. Imagine someone who repeatedly breaks a promise despite sincerely endorsing it. Changes in surroundings, practiced routines and help from others may alter the outcome. Augustine’s attention to divided motivation remains useful; whether divine grace is required is not settled by the description or the improvement. Equally, showing that ordinary causes matter would not alone refute a theology that regards them as instruments of grace. The disagreement concerns what evidence discriminates between explanations.
listItems: Best objection: Psychological recognition does not establish theological necessity. The claim that human conflict requires a particular account of sin and grace carries an additional burden of justification.

Charitable reply: Augustine does not offer one autobiographical episode as an isolated proof of Christianity. His interpretation draws on a wider theological argument; a critic should identify which premises they reject.
Contemporary test: In the promise-breaking example, distinguish knowing the obligation, wanting to comply and sustaining compliance. Evidence about one does not automatically explain the others.

Charitable reply under pressure: Grace can be described as enabling voluntary action rather than coercing it. That answers one objection, but leaves questions about responsibility, unequal assistance and the conditions of blame.

Contemporary test of the inference: Ask what a rival explanation would lead us to expect differently. If all possible outcomes are compatible with a proposed explanation, its power to distinguish alternatives needs further defense.

sections.heading: Begin with the divided will, then widen the inquiry
paragraphs: Begin with Confessions VIII, especially the movement from established habit to conflicting wills and the final conversion scene. Read the scene within the book’s address to God. Separate three questions in your notes: what Augustine says he experienced, how he interprets it, and which reasons a reader has for accepting that interpretation. This preserves both the psychological interest and the religious purpose.

Then read selected passages from books X and XI: the exploration of memory, the distinction between memory, attention and expectation, and the example of reciting a song. Try that last example slowly. Notice how anticipation and recollection change while the song progresses. The exercise gives a foothold in the argument without resolving the metaphysics of time.

For a contrasting form of argument, turn to On Free Choice of the Will, a dialogue about evil and responsibility, and then the later On Grace and Free Will. The titles are similar but refer to different works. Read them with their different contexts in mind rather than assuming Augustine’s treatment of freedom never developed. Keep the original question in view: which aspects of responsible agency can introspection clarify, and which require further evidence or argument?
listItems: Best entry point: Why do human beings so often know the better and still choose the worse? Begin with an actual passage about conflict rather than treating the phrase “divided will” as its explanation.
What to watch: The confessional voice reports, interprets and prays. Those activities can support one another without supplying the same kind of evidence.

Where to go next: Follow the dispute from Confessions to the works on free choice and grace. The issue is whether dependence on help can coexist with responsibility, not merely whether the word “freedom” appears.

Reading discipline: Compare passages before attributing a single unchanging position to a writer whose concerns and controversies developed. Preserve the distinction between an early work and a later reply.

Avoid the shortcut: Neither “he invented the modern self” nor “it is only theology” captures the combination of inward description, argument and religious interpretation. Assess those contributions separately.

synthesisHeading: An illuminating account can still leave its explanation disputed
synthesisParagraphs: Augustine’s divided will makes a person’s endorsement of a course of action different from their ability to follow it wholeheartedly. His work on memory and time similarly complicates the idea that the mind simply sees itself without difficulty.

The critical question is how far those observations support his theological conclusions. Taking the observations seriously does not require treating grace as proved; rejecting that conclusion does not erase the questions about agency and self-understanding.
Use the five follow-up questions below to examine a particular passage about conflict, memory or time. Identify both what the passage reveals and what its interpretation would need to establish.
references:
Primary texts for this revision

The English translations below provide access to Augustine’s arguments. The profile’s comparisons and criticisms are editorial interpretations, not quotations.

  • Confessions I: desire and its religious interpretation.
  • Confessions VIII: habit, conflicting wills and conversion.
  • Confessions X: memory and self-understanding.
  • Confessions XI: temporal awareness and the recitation example.
  • On Grace and Free Will: voluntary action and divine assistance.
